title: Libraries and Utilities Technical Reference
summary: Shared-code review is stricter because a small change can affect startup, requests, pipelines, imports, jobs, events, and tests.

sections.heading: Purpose and ownership
items: Libraries and utilities provide small reusable technical behavior with no independent business authority. They support modules but do not own schemas, routes, persistence, permissions, or workflow decisions.

A library encapsulates a cohesive reusable contract; a utility is a narrow stateless helper. If behavior needs lifecycle, configuration, provider selection, audit, or domain ownership, use an appropriate service instead.
Place shared code at the lowest layer that owns the abstraction and avoid circular dependencies or a generic dumping ground.

sections.heading: Design rules
items: Functions use explicit inputs and outputs, deterministic behavior where possible, stable error contracts, null and boundary handling, and no hidden global mutation.
Do not read process environment, database, cache, request context, or secrets inside a generic helper unless that access is the declared owned abstraction.
Avoid prototype mutation, unsafe object-path writes, uncontrolled recursion, dynamic evaluation, and logging of caller payloads.

sections.heading: Customization
items: Prefer configuration or service extension over copying a utility. A customer override must preserve callers' contract or use a new explicitly versioned function.
Keep module-private helpers inside the owning module until multiple real consumers establish a stable shared abstraction.
Document parameters, return values, errors, mutability, complexity, security assumptions, examples, and unsupported input next to the implementation.

sections.heading: Runtime and performance
items: Hot-path utilities avoid repeated allocation, serialization, regular-expression compilation, and unbounded traversal, but correctness and clarity precede speculative optimization.
Asynchronous helpers propagate cancellation, timeout, correlation, and errors instead of swallowing them or creating detached work.
Caching inside a helper requires explicit ownership, complete keys, bounded memory, invalidation, and testability; otherwise use the framework cache contract.

sections.heading: Verification
items: Test normal, empty, null, malformed, boundary, large, malicious, concurrent, and immutable-input behavior with focused unit tests.
Add integration tests when a helper shapes router, schema, security, import, provider, or lifecycle behavior, and regression tests for every fixed defect.
Review dependency direction, duplicate implementations, dead exports, compatibility, documentation, licensing, and generated-context visibility before release.

sections.heading: Checklist
items: Owner, consumers, purpose, input/output, determinism, side effects, and complexity.
Explicit context, dependencies, errors, trace propagation, security, and performance.
Capability-specific versus framework-wide placement justification.
Extension, compatibility, deprecation, and migration policy.
Positive, invalid-input, boundary, error-propagation, concurrency, performance, and consumer-regression tests.
